title: Choose how cw-code occupies the screen
question: These directions change the workspace mechanism itself. Choose one to turn into three precise compositions, or re-roll the set.

options.label: Session Ribbon
options.lineage: browser tab strips, terminal multiplexers, and a machinist's movable tool tray
options.thesis: The active conversation owns the screen; every running session stays visible in a horizontal ribbon and every tool arrives as a dockable tray.
options.viewport: A slim project rail at left, a grouped live-session ribbon across the top, one wide chat stage, and a bottom tool tray that can be dragged to any edge or split into the stage.
options.risk: A long ribbon needs excellent grouping and overflow behavior once dozens of sessions are open.

raised.raise: The active session title earns monumental scale while supporting text becomes nearly silent.
Dragging a dock transforms the whole work plane instead of opening another bordered panel.
Running, waiting, and approval states use explicit labelled controls rather than ambiguous icon chrome.
Every project and session remains directly reachable by keyboard without navigating intermediate panels.
High-density telemetry collapses into one peripheral activity rhythm rather than more prose.

options.label: T3 Switchboard
options.lineage: T3 Code's session hierarchy with editor modes rather than permanent tool columns
options.thesis: Projects and sessions stay in one calm navigator; Thread, Files, Diff, Agents, and Terminal take turns owning the same work surface.
options.viewport: A T3-like project/session navigator remains at left while the rest of the window is one mode-switching stage; the composer stays anchored only in Thread mode and tools can be pinned into a split when needed.
options.risk: The familiar direction is the least visually surprising and temporarily hides the conversation when a tool takes over.

options.label: Live Project Board
options.lineage: Metro typographic tiles translated into a multi-project operations board
options.thesis: Projects are color fields, sessions are live typographic tiles, and the selected tile expands into a working conversation without opening a conventional pane.
options.viewport: A horizontally pannable project board fills the window; one selected session tile expands to two-thirds width as the chat while neighboring live sessions remain readable at the edge.
options.case: It makes multi-session work more visible than the lead and removes panel chrome, but long-form chat is less naturally calm.
options.risk: Without disciplined restraint it could feel like a dashboard rather than a coding workspace.

options.label: Command Weather
options.thesis: Session activity becomes a typographic field whose words gather around the currently active work.
options.viewport: Large session names drift into a command surface and condense into the selected conversation.
options.case: The metaphor weakens task scanability and makes operational state feel decorative.
options.risk: The active animation would compete with reading and code inspection.

options.label: Elastic Workspace
options.thesis: One uninterrupted work plane gathers into named docks when the developer pulls a handle toward an edge.
options.viewport: The conversation begins full screen and physically folds to make room for a dragged file, diff, agent, or terminal dock.
options.case: The transform interaction is strong but the garment metaphor does not help developers identify the product.
options.kept: Docking changes the composition instead of adding another box.
options.risk: The literal pull gesture could be less discoverable than normal resizing.

options.label: Session Mixer
options.thesis: Every active session becomes a channel with a compact state meter and a tactile focus switch.
options.viewport: A thin session mixer runs along the bottom while the selected channel opens as the full conversation above it.
options.case: It communicates simultaneous activity well but its skeuomorphism distracts from the actual CLI content.
options.kept: Every state and action should feel labelled, tactile, and unambiguous.
options.risk: The fascia can become control-heavy and visually nostalgic.

options.label: Direct Address
options.thesis: Projects and sessions have direct keyboard addresses and the entire shell behaves like a fast page service.
options.viewport: A sparse session index occupies the left quarter and addressed work pages replace the remaining field instantly.
options.case: Direct access is valuable, but the fixed broadcast grid fights prose, code, and adjustable desktop density.
options.kept: Everything important receives a direct keyboard route.
options.risk: The retro language would overwhelm cw-code's product identity.

options.label: Activity Field
options.thesis: All concurrent sessions become one peripheral activity field and the selected stream resolves into readable work.
options.viewport: A narrow activity field visualizes every session at once beside one large selected thread.
options.case: It excels at ambient monitoring but hides the names and semantics developers need to choose the next session.
options.kept: Dense telemetry should read peripherally before it expands into detail.
options.risk: Pure data abstraction would make the workspace harder to learn.

canonCard.label: Conventional IDE Shell
canonCard.thesis: A project sidebar, central conversation, persistent right inspector, and bottom status bar executed cleanly.
canonCard.viewport: The familiar VS Code and T3 hybrid: three persistent columns with resizable separators.
canonCard.risk: It is structurally the same answer already rejected and asks borders to explain too much.
